title: Can one shared world hold different foregrounds?
question: Can TurtleBlock AI support a shared world in which different collaborators keep distinct attention agendas—and sometimes choose to share or negotiate them—without collapsing everyone into one machine-selected foreground?
why_now: The September 12 Selective Attention Envelope makes single-context attention governance inspectable: an observable event is not automatically retained, salient, surfaced, interrupt-worthy, or important; learner-authored watchpoints can authorize interruption; Turtle salience remains a proposal; deliberate silence is valid; and attention cannot expand collection. That immediately exposes the collaborative problem. The same bridge collapse, crowd movement, timing result, or improvised event can matter differently to different people. Minecraft Education continues to emphasize multiple learner strategies and collaborative agent design; NVIDIA's newest workflow shows that participants can possess consequential context unavailable to a model; OpenAI's full-duplex work makes listening, pausing, and interrupting explicit interaction decisions; and MIT's jam_bot work shows reciprocal creative collaboration where timing and foreground are part of the interaction itself. The next horizon is therefore not a smarter shared alert system. It is whether a shared computational world can preserve several legitimate foregrounds at once without Turtle averaging, broadcasting, surveilling, or silently deciding what the group ought to care about.
inputs: September 12 Selective Attention Envelope schema and eight-case hostile regression suite
September 12 successful GitHub Actions validation run
September 11 World Evidence Envelope and selective-noticing residue
September 10 Learner Verification Card and regression suite
Turtle Terraria provenance, evidence-class, privacy, and capture-batch boundaries
Sanders immutable dissertation Dedoose source layer and later ontology layers
seven established Critical Techno Constructivism operational domains
STEAMHAMLET, Purposeful Play, constructionism, Possible Possibles, and Co-active Emergence lineage
Turtle Charter rules on agency, disagreement, plurality, reflection, reversibility, and human judgment
September 12 primary-source hunt across OpenAI, NVIDIA, Minecraft Education, and MIT Media Lab
September 12 uncaptured residue concerning salience, restraint, bounded project attention, and multiple foregrounds
possible_possibles: Each collaborator keeps a private attention layer over the same shared world and chooses which watchpoints, if any, become visible to others.
A shared event can surface immediately to one learner, remain silent for another, and be deferred for a third without treating those different foregrounds as inconsistency.
Collaborators explicitly negotiate a temporary shared watchpoint such as 'tell all of us if the bridge collapses' while unrelated personal attention rules remain private.
Turtle exposes an attention conflict instead of averaging it: one participant wants speed foregrounded while another wants access, aesthetics, ecological impact, or nothing at all foregrounded.
A participant can share the reason for a watchpoint without revealing the underlying private project history that made it important.
A world event becomes a collaborative question only after participants choose to bring their different interpretations or attention priorities into the same conversation.
A Recursive Turtle Terrarium generates synthetic multi-participant attention conflicts as regression material, clearly labeled synthetic_self_play and unable to promote its own policy.
The group intentionally keeps no shared foreground at all for a period of purposeful play, allowing each participant to wander before deciding what deserves collective attention.
x_factor: whoooo knooooowwwssssssssssss — what if the same collapsing bridge is urgent to one learner, delightful to another, and none of Turtle's business to a third?
constraints: The Next Edge points beyond the completed Selective Attention Envelope and does not merely add more single-user attention fields.
A shared world must not imply a shared attention agenda by default.
One participant's watchpoint, purpose, interpretation, or urgency must not silently become another participant's curriculum.
Private attention rules and project history are not automatically visible to collaborators merely because the world is shared.
Participants should be able to share, revise, withdraw, mute, or negotiate collaborative attention rules when practical.
Turtle may help expose attention disagreement but must not average meaningful disagreement into synthetic consensus.
The easiest event to measure must not become the group's most important event by default.
World events, participant attention rules, Turtle proposals, surfacing decisions, interpretations, and later group decisions retain distinct provenance.
Synthetic self-play remains synthetic_self_play and has no production authority.
No generalized persistent personal memory is introduced by this horizon.
No autonomous production self-modification or self-retraining is authorized.
Environment configuration may contribute metadata only; private configuration values are never inspected, inferred, recorded, or published.
New CTC domains remain provisional observations until an explicit human scholarly decision promotes one.

ontology_mappings.rationale: Several human participants, Turtle, and the shared world may reciprocally alter what becomes meaningful; preserving distinct foregrounds prevents co-active emergence from being reduced to one machine-normalized group state.
Different participants may notice different consequences during shared play, and a group should be able to remain exploratory without Turtle forcing one collective reflection agenda.
Distinct participant foregrounds can preserve several possible directions at once instead of converting shared space into a single ranked task list.
Turtle's choices about whose watchpoint to surface, defer, or mediate should themselves remain inspectable rather than becoming invisible group authority.
Participant-specific attention priorities and conflicts can become explicit enough to inspect and negotiate without forcing their private rationale into a public shared state.
A room of possibilities is richer when several inhabitants can move through the same environment with different questions and foregrounds rather than receiving one system-authored narration.
A shared world can hold many participant attention rules only if authorship, privacy, evidence class, surfacing decisions, and later negotiation remain distinguishable.
Different participants may enter reflection and revision from different events or at different times; the recursive loop need not synchronize everyone into one machine-selected moment.

ctc_mappings.rationale: A shared environment should preserve each participant's ability to pursue and revise their own inquiry rather than letting shared infrastructure overwrite individual purpose.
An event can become a collective problem when participants choose to bring it into shared inquiry, while remaining irrelevant or differently meaningful to others.

ctc_mappings.domain: Technology as Tool to Think With
ctc_mappings.rationale: Inspectable participant-specific and shared attention layers could make the computational foreground itself a manipulable object-to-think-with rather than an opaque group recommendation engine.
Changes in what collaborators choose to watch, share, dispute, or ignore may eventually expose evolving inquiry, but those system records are not automatically evidence that learning occurred.
Collaborators should be able to reflect on different observations and on the disagreement among their foregrounds without Turtle imposing a single reflective timetable or conclusion.
Shared attention governance makes power visible: whose concerns are broadcast, whose remain private, which metrics dominate, and who gets interrupted are socially consequential design choices.
The horizon directly asks how collaborators can intentionally share or negotiate attention while preserving difference, privacy, disagreement, and authorship.

uncaptured_residue.observation: Collaborative attention has both individual and collective states: the same event may be privately salient, jointly salient, or deliberately unshared, and those states may change without the world event itself changing.
uncaptured_residue.reason_unmapped: The seven CTC domains describe inquiry, reflection, critique, and collaboration but do not directly specify a privacy-aware foreground layer that can be individual and collective at the same time.

uncaptured_residue.observation: Negotiating a shared foreground may itself become a learning artifact, but forcing every attention disagreement into explicit negotiation could burden collaboration and destroy the value of tacit wandering.
uncaptured_residue.reason_unmapped: This tension sits between Sharing and Collaborating, Personal Inquiry, and purposeful play; it may be a design principle rather than a new learner-development domain.

uncaptured_residue.observation: A participant may wish to reveal that an event matters without revealing why it matters, creating a provenance requirement for selective disclosure rather than simple public/private classification.
uncaptured_residue.reason_unmapped: Current privacy classes describe an object's visibility but do not yet model partial disclosure of attention rationale inside a shared inquiry.
